content: The following is a professional summary of the declarations and findings related to tuberculosis (TB) research and treatment guidelines: 1. Funding and Declarations of Interest: Daniela Cirillo received funding from the World Health Organization (WHO) for consultancies and travel, as well as grants from the Global Fund and TB-REACH to cover 10% of her salary. She also received funding from FIND to evaluate drug-susceptibility testing (DST) for new drugs and from Otsuka to evaluate DST for delamanid. She leads a supranational TB reference laboratory in Italy, focusing on capacity-building for DST technologies for second-line drugs and new diagnostics for drug-resistant TB. Additionally, she is a member of the Italian national committee for the use of bedaquiline. Charles L. Daley received funding from Otsuka to chair the data monitoring committee for delamanid trials, totaling $47,000 over seven years. Kelly Dooley received funding to provide expert advice on trial design for TB/HIV studies, with $2,000 per year paid to her employer. She co-chairs an AIDS Clinical Trials Group (ACTG) study on bedaquiline and delamanid, serves as principal investigator for trials assessing pretomanid, and participates in studies on high-dose isoniazid for MDR-TB, rifapentine for latent TB in pregnant women and children, and bedaquiline and delamanid for children with MDR-TB and HIV. Agnes Gebhard works for the KNCV TB Foundation, which has projects funded by the Eli Lilly Foundation to engage the private sector in TB diagnosis and treatment and to roll out the QuanTB drug forecasting tool. KNCV also collaborates with Cepheid on GeneXpert machine installation and training in Nigeria and Vietnam. Carlos Torres-Duque received honoraria from Janssen Pharmaceuticals for presentations on TB prevention and WHO policy on bedaquiline at a 2014 Latin American MDR-TB meeting. Tom Shinnick, an employee of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), declared that his travel and research related to TB laboratory services were supported by the CDC. He served on the Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) for a delamanid trial organized by Otsuka but did not receive remuneration for this role. 2. Conflicts of Interest and Recusals: Lindsay McKenna, employed by the Treatment Action Group (TAG), received non-commercial support from various organizations, including the Stop TB Partnership and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. She was recused from discussions on MDR-TB regimen composition during a 2015 meeting. José Caminero, a consultant for the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease (UNION), was recused from discussions on shorter MDR-TB regimens during a 2015 meeting. 3. External Review Group (ERG) and Evidence Reviewers: Several ERG members declared no conflicts of interest, while others declared interests judged not to conflict with the meeting objectives. For example, Guy Marks received research support from AERAS and serves as Vice-President of the UNION and Editor-in-Chief of the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease. Evidence reviewers, including Matthew Arentz and Carole Mitnick, presented findings at the meeting but did not participate in formulating recommendations. 4. WHO Guidelines and Evidence Summaries: The WHO guidelines for the programmatic management of drug-resistant TB were updated with funding from the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID). The experts involved contributed their time to discussions and activities. The guidelines evaluated the efficacy and safety of shorter, all-oral regimens containing bedaquiline for MDR/RR-TB patients compared to longer regimens with injectables or without new TB drugs. The evidence was of very low certainty, with outcomes showing modest improvements in success rates and reductions in loss to follow-up. For XDR-TB or treatment-intolerant MDR-TB patients, a 6–9 month regimen of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid was compared to longer regimens. The evidence suggested potential benefits but remained of very low certainty. 5. Research and Clinical Trials: Studies on shorter regimens, including those containing bedaquiline and linezolid, were conducted to improve outcomes for TB patients. The findings highlighted the need for further research to address gaps in evidence and improve treatment strategies. This detailed account reflects the contributions, funding sources, and potential conflicts of interest among experts involved in TB research and guideline development. It underscores the collaborative efforts to advance TB treatment while maintaining transparency and addressing conflicts of interest.
